title: The ghetto
hookLine: Venice walls in its Jews in 1516, the first ghetto

cards: The guard at the gate is paid by the people he locks in. Each evening in Venice, as bells ring across the water, he swings a heavy gate shut on one small island in the city.
Behind it, Jewish families settle in for the night. They may go out by day to trade, to work, to see a patient. After dark, by law, they must be inside.
In the morning the gate opens again. Across the canal, the rest of the city goes about its evening. Today, the ghetto.

teach.b: The Republic of Venice allowed Jews to live in the city, but only in one enclosed area.

Some say the name ghetto comes from a foundry that once stood there; whatever its source, the word stuck, and it later spread to enclosed Jewish quarters in other cities. The rules were simple and hard.
Guards at the gates, paid, as we heard, by the Jews themselves. Jews needed permission to live in Venice at all, and the permission had to be renewed.
Because the area could not grow outward, the buildings grew upward, story on story, crowded and tall. And yet look inside the walls.
Synagogues were tucked into the upper floors of ordinary buildings, so that from the street you might never know they were there.
Different communities kept their own: Jews from Germany, from Italy, from Spain and Portugal and the East, each with its own melody and custom, side by side in a few crowded streets.
Printers in Venice produced Hebrew books. Scholars taught and preached. Life went on, behind a gate.
The Psalms have a blessing for walls: "Peace be within thy walls." The psalm means the walls of Jerusalem, walls that protect. The ghetto's walls were built by others, to keep a people apart.
Both are true of this place: a cage from outside, and inside, a home that people made anyway. The word ghetto would later be used for far darker places.
That is part of why today's line is said plainly: walls around people.

how: The old ghetto of Venice still has working synagogues and a Jewish museum, and Jews visiting the city often go to pray or remember there.

games.q: you are a Jewish family in Venice. you may live only in the walled quarter, which cannot grow. what happens?
o: families move out to the countryside.
the buildings grow upward, story on story.
the city widens the quarter every year.
games.why: unable to grow outward, the ghetto grew upward, with tall, crowded buildings.

practice: Bring to mind any wall you know of, real or invisible, that keeps a group of people apart: a fence, a rule, a neighborhood line, a door that only some can open.
See the people on the other side making a home inside it, then the faces of the ones who built it, and hold both in view.

wordCard.voice: The ghetto. The walled Jewish quarter of Venice, gated at night, where Jews were kept apart and still built synagogues, printing and a life of their own. Today's word.

orig.note: chomah is the Hebrew word for a wall, like a city wall.

carryVoice: Your line: walls around people. Behind the gate, they built a life anyway. Until tomorrow.
